Stage 3 · Reading

The language you can hear across a valley

On one Canary island a whole conversation crosses two kilometres of empty air — and the brain treats it as speech.

🏝️💭
1 · Before you read. Look at the title and the photograph. What kind of place do you expect?

Choose one and say what it would have to do with whistling. Compare with a partner.Choose one and say what it would have to do with whistling.Choose one and note what it would have to do with whistling.

The language you can hear across a valley

Written for this course, from the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listing for Silbo Gomero (2009) and Carreiras, López, Rivero & Corina, ‘Neural processing of a whistled language’, Nature 433 (2005).

1Most travellers have never heard of La Gomera, and those who have usually know it for one extraordinary thing. The island is the worn tip of an old volcano, cut through by ravines so deep and slopes so steep that two farms facing each other across a valley can be an hour apart on foot. Long before there were roads, the islanders solved that problem in a way that still sounds improbable. They learned to whistle their language across it.

2Silbo Gomero is not a code, and it is not a set of agreed signals for danger or dinner. It consists of a small set of whistled sounds that stand for the vowels and consonants of ordinary Spanish: two whistles carry all five vowels, four more carry the consonants, and the ear separates them by pitch and by whether the sound is continuous or broken. Because the system consists of sounds rather than of ready-made messages, and maps onto the language itself, anything an islander can say, an islander can whistle. A skilled whistler is understood two or three kilometres away, across country that would take most of a morning to cross. At that distance, with the wind moving, visitors regularly mistake it for birdsong.

3Nobody is certain where it came from. Most accounts point to North Africa, and when Spanish replaced the older island tongue the whistle was simply adapted to the new language and carried on, as it adapts to any change in the speech around it. It belonged, for ages, to shepherds and to anyone else whose working day was spent on a hillside. It has one built-in weakness: a whistled signal contains far less information than a spoken one, so the same whistle can correspond to several different words. That ambiguity results in genuine mistakes, and whistlers deal with it the way readers deal with a difficult sentence — by repeating, and by relying on context.

4By the middle of the twentieth century it was in trouble. Roads, telephones and emigration all contributed to its decline, and it acquired a reputation as something rural and backward. Plenty of islanders disapproved of it, and a good number were embarrassed by it: it belonged, they felt, to the poverty their children were escaping. Visitors who had heard of it expected folklore — a ukulele in a hotel lobby, a performance for tourists rather than a working language. By the 1980s the last fluent whistlers were mostly old men.

5What rescued it was not enthusiasm but policy. In 1999 the island authorities made Silbo a compulsory subject in every primary and secondary school on La Gomera, and that decision has resulted in something no earlier attempt achieved: a whole generation that grew up whistling in class. In 2009 UNESCO added Silbo Gomero to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, describing it as the only whistled language in the world that is fully developed and practised by a large community — on an island of some 22,000 people.

6The most interesting evidence came from a laboratory. In 2005 a team led by Manuel Carreiras published a study in Nature that scanned the brains of fluent whistlers while they listened to Silbo. In those whistlers, the regions that normally handle speech responded to the whistles exactly as they respond to words. In Spanish speakers who could not whistle, the same sounds resulted in nothing of the kind: the brain filed them as noise. Language, it turns out, does not depend on the mouth. It adapts to whatever channel the landscape leaves open — and on La Gomera the landscape left the air.

Text A · A language made of whistles

Written for this course, from the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listing for Silbo Gomero (2009).

Most travellers have never heard of La Gomera, and those who have usually know it for one extraordinary thing. A skilled whistler is understood two or three kilometres away, across country that would take most of a morning to cross. At that distance, with the wind moving, visitors regularly mistake it for birdsong.

Nobody is certain where it came from. Most accounts point to North Africa, and when Spanish replaced the older island tongue the whistle was simply adapted to the new language and carried on, as it adapts to any change in the speech around it. Text B · Nearly lost, then legislated back

Written for this course, from the UNESCO listing (2009) and Carreiras, López, Rivero & Corina, Nature 433 (2005).

By the middle of the twentieth century Silbo was in trouble. Roads, telephones and emigration all contributed to its decline, and it acquired a reputation as something rural and backward. Plenty of islanders disapproved of it, and a good number were embarrassed by it: it belonged, they felt, to the poverty their children were escaping. In 1999 the island authorities made Silbo a compulsory subject in every primary and secondary school on La Gomera, and that decision has resulted in something no earlier attempt achieved: a whole generation that grew up whistling in class. Verbs and their prepositions

Some verbs will not stand alone. The preposition is part of the meaning, not decoration.

2 · Answer the three questions about the lines above.

3 · Read the table.
Verb + prepositionMeaningExample
consist ofbe made up of — the complete contentsThe course consists of four modules.
contribute tobe one cause among severalEmigration contributed to the decline.
adapt tochange to suit a new situationShe soon adapted to island life.
disapprove ofthink something is wrongThey disapproved of the whole idea.

After the preposition comes a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form — never an infinitive. It resulted in losing the contract, not it resulted in to lose.

4 · The pairs that catch people out.
I’ve never heard of her.  →  I don’t know she exists.
I haven’t heard from her.  →  She hasn’t been in touch.

1 · Read the explanation.
Why the preposition matters

Some verbs need a preposition before their object, and the preposition is fixed: you cannot reason your way to it. Consist always takes of; result takes in or from, and the choice reverses the meaning. Learn each verb together with its preposition, as one item.

Whatever follows the preposition must be a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form — never an infinitive: It resulted in losing the contract, not resulted in to lose.

The pairs that reverse meaning
  • result in vs result from. The delay resulted in extra costs (delay → costs). The extra costs resulted from the delay (costs ← delay).
  • hear of vs hear from. I’ve never heard of her (I don’t know she exists). I haven’t heard from her (she hasn’t written).
  • adapt to vs adapt for. She adapted to the climate (she changed). She adapted the text for children (the text changed).
  • contribute to vs cause. Contribute to admits other causes; cause claims the whole responsibility.
2 · Study the examples.
PatternExample
consist of + nounThe island consists of a single ridge and two valleys.
consist of + -ingHis job consists of answering the phone.
contribute to + nounThree factors contributed to the decision.
contribute to + -ingThe programme contributed to saving the language.
adapt to + nounIt took her a year to adapt to the climate.
adapt something forThey adapted the novel for the stage.
disapprove of + nounHer parents disapproved of the marriage.
disapprove of + -ingHe disapproves of interrupting people.
hear of + nounHave you heard of Silbo Gomero?
hear from + personI haven’t heard from my brother for ages.
result in + nounThe storm resulted in serious damage.
result in + -ingThe error resulted in losing the whole file.
result from + nounThe damage resulted from the storm.
depend on + nounEverything depends on the weather.
belong to + personThat notebook belongs to me.
apply for + nounShe applied for the teaching post.
Two things to watch

1 — No preposition at all. Some verbs that look as though they need one do not: discuss (not discuss about), enter (not enter into a room), answer (not answer to a question), reach (not reach to).

2 — Passive keeps the preposition. The whistle was adapted to Spanish. The preposition stays attached to the verb even when the object moves to the front.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
The preposition is part of the verb

With consist of, contribute to, adapt to, approve of, object to, result in, lead to, hear of the preposition carries no meaning of its own. It is simply the form the verb takes before its complement, and leaving it out is an error, not an informality: The course consists four modules.

Whatever follows the preposition must be a noun or an -ing form — never a to-infinitive: They objected to paying in advance, not objected to pay. This catches learners out most with object to and adapt to, where the to looks like an infinitive marker and is not.

In questions and relative clauses the preposition normally stays where the verb left it: What does the fee consist of? · the decision we objected to. Moving it to the front (Of what does the fee consist?) is possible but sounds legal rather than spoken.

Same verb, different preposition, different meaning

result in points forward to the consequence (The strike resulted in heavy losses); result from points back to the cause (The losses resulted from the strike). The same reversal runs through lead to and contribute to — both point forward, both take the consequence, not the cause.

hear of means know that somebody or something exists; hear from means receive news from them; hear about means learn the details. I have never heard of her and I have not heard from her are entirely different complaints.

Errors to watch: consist from → consist of · discuss about it → discuss it · explain me the rule → explain the rule to me · answer to the question → answer the question · She is consisting of — consist is a state verb and takes no continuous.

1 · Read the model.
Model

Most people outside the region have never heard of the reed flutes my grandfather’s village made, and I only know about them because a box of them sat in his workshop for ages.

The craft consisted of two things: cutting reeds from one particular bend of the river, and drying them through a whole winter before anybody touched a knife. Nothing about it was quick. Three things contributed to its end. The river was straightened in the 1970s and the reed beds went with it. The younger men left for the city and did not come back. And the flutes themselves acquired a reputation as something rural, which younger families quietly disapproved of.

A museum now runs a summer workshop, and that has resulted in perhaps forty people a year learning to cut a reed. I am not sure what to call this. It is not the craft my grandfather adapted to a changing market. It is a memory of it, kept warm.
